title: Night at the Junkyard
author: Dandelion
imageAlt: Cover image for Night at the Junkyard

runs.text: My mind wanders back to a serene winter night. In a land that is no more, yet exists in a thousand minds.

I was somewhere around five, with an elder as my guide. We went to pick up trash, from an overgrown yard. A fire burned in the middle: dancing in the wind, like the effervescent rhythm of a long-forgotten rhyme. We chattered, while collecting trash; dropping each into the pit. I gazed, mesmerized, at how things transformed in heat. A sandal half torn, clinging barely to its sole; I wondered of each forsaken: what stories did it withhold?

We overturned the burning sandal, and a secret was revealed. Beneath it clung a spiral: the shell of a being. We had hoped it long abandoned. Alas, we were deceived. The shell spiraled backwards, pushing out the occupant within. It had four protruding eyes; how innocent they seemed! Its skin gleamed like marble, against the light of the flame. Alas, I couldn't save it; it boiled before my eyes. My breathing drew thin, for every soul felt like kin.

The stars twinkled careless, scattered across the sky. The cold blew at the edges, lingering outside the warmth. A field overrun by foliage, hiding long-neglected remains. We burnt away the traces, killing stories unheard.

runs.text: The Man Who Reached The Void
There are questions that haunt humanity, and there are questions that consume those who are
foolish enough to pursue them.
For Marcus, there was only one.
“After everything ends, where do we go?”
This is a story about the man who uncovered the secrets of consciousness and what lies beyond
death, Marcus Ashford. His life was shaped by early tragedy. At twelve, he watched his mother
succumb to Alzheimer’s disease. Her mind slowly deteriorated and eventually death followed. The
funeral was over, and the house had begun to forget. By evening, everything had gone quiet. The
silence was so peaceful it felt like it was mocking his sorrow. He began to understand the odd
cruelty of being human. Marcus found his father sitting beneath the dim light of the living room.
Dad, is this the end?”
“Marcus, you think we have lost her, don’t you? That she had slipped into some great void-
something unreachable”
“But isn’t that how it works,dad?”
“Not really. You must’ve learned about the law of conservation of energy. But energy isn’t
necessarily consciousness”
“So, mother’s brain used electrical signals and chemical reactions to process memories,
emotions, and thoughts. And when it stopped functioning, those processes ended. The energy
involved was transferred into other forms”
“Yes, you’re precisely right, and we can also measure the processes regarding these neural
activities, yet we don’t understand how these physical processes begin and end, and forms our
consciousness or that if this consciousness of ours, survive death”
“So mum could still be out there, somewhere?”
“Perhaps,son. Perhaps there’s a heaven and somewhere beyond the stars she is no longer lost to
time
Marcus found comfort in a place that might only exist because he needed it to.
By 2035, his obsession had materialized into
The Horizon
, a spacecraft engineered to explore the
edge of consciousness. Its quantum settings were designed to read through dark matter and a
field generator for understanding hypothetical negative energy states. And the negative energy
could be stabilised to allow the spacecraft’s traversable speed to match the light’s speed. It was
perfectly engineered to contract distances between any two points, altering space geometry and
equipped with quantum sensors—that could trace anomalous neural activity and energies
associated with consciousness. In May 2040,
The Horizon
embarked on its first mission. Marcus
along with his teammates, constantly checked the vacuum fluctuations, gravitational
disturbances, and deviations in quantum energies. But their main objective was to flag anomalies.
The spacecraft navigated through nebulas and black holes, crossing light-years of space in mere
days. By August 2040, Marcus reached a region that had gradual disappearance of cosmic
radiation. The sensors recorded a decrease in energy as stars and galaxies faded from view,
leaving only darkness. The ship’s sensors, designed to measure even the faintest energy
fluctuations, showed nothing. Undeterred, Marcus pushed forward. The spacecraft, equipped with
high-resolution quantum detectors, ventured deeper into the anomalous region, his whole life
leading to this very moment. Marcus analyzed the readings but the results were unclear, complete
silence. There were no energy traces, no quantum disturbances—nothing. Driven by hope to see if
his mother was still out there somewhere, Marcus decided to push “
The Horizon
” deeper into the
darkness until a surge of light enveloped him fully that seemed to wrap reality itself. The ship
disintegrated slowly. Atoms unravelled and the fabric of space and time collapsed. Marcus felt the
same unravelling in his own body. This place held the source of all the meanings he had been
searching for his entire life. It felt cold and bright. It wasn’t necessarily heaven, not an afterlife but
felt like something closer to a void. At that moment, he found out, the source of all meanings. And
so Marcus realised that it was nothing, just a void which held no answers. Something inside
Marcus quietly gave way. He realised that it wasn’t the source of all the meaning that he had been
chasing his whole life. It wasn’t about discovering continuity after death or his mother; it was
merely having something to live for, just as all humans require a driving force to go on.As the light
around him dissolved, he returned.
2nd December, 2040, marked the day Marcus would make his final public appearance about his
discovery. He was agitated. His father stood in the doorway, older now. For a moment, neither
spoke.
“You think you have lost, don’t you, Marcus? That you’ve found a place you can’t reach. But that’s
not how it works”
Marcus stared at the floor,
“I thought, somewhere in all that darkness, there would be something
that held all the answers to my grief and give meaning to my hope”
“You are not grieving your mother,Marcus. You are becoming her”
Marcus stared at his father
“You haven’t realized it yet. You have not lost your mother. Every tear, every action, every
moment of joy or sorrow, it’s her finding ways to remain inside you. You are a part of her, her
legacy
But dad-“
“Feel it Marcus. All of it, the grief, the sorrow,the anger, the very process of being hollowed out
and let it reshape you”
Marcus nodded, the weight of his father’s word settling inside him.
His father trailed off, “
And when you’ve become someone new, you’ll find that it’s not all that
miserable, at all. You don’t have to let go of your mother, son. You just have to keep living”
For a moment Marcus felt sad, but then strangely happy. Then, with a reassuring smile he walked
out. Outside, In front of an auditorium, packed with people who were eager to know what he had
uncovered, he stepped onto the stage and answered.

content: অ-মানুষ
'এইখানে রাতে আসতে কোনো মানুষ সাহস করে না, যারা ভুলেও এসে পরসে, তারা আমার পেটে. তুমি কে?

পাশের হোটেলের থেইকা একটা মাছ আর কোনোরকম দুইমুঠ ভাত চুরি কইরা, গ্রাম থেইকা একটু দূরে এই নির্জন জাগায় আইসি শান্তি কইরা খাইতে. ইজাগায় নাকি কারো বাপেও সাহস করে না যাইতে, বিশেষ কইরা রাইতে এক রক্ত খেকো নাকি ঘরে দুইটা লোকরে কইতে শুনলাম। কিন্তু ধরা না খাইতে আমি সাহস করলাম, একটা খাতের বেড়া টপকে ওই নির্জন গ্রামে ঢুকে পড়লাম। এখানে  একটু  পরপর নির্জন  কতগুলা  ভাঙা  বাড়ি , তারই যেকোনো একটায় ঢুকে একোনায় বসে  চুরি করা  খাবার ঠোঙা থেকে খাইতেসিলাম  এর  মধ্যে  একটা বিশাল কিছুটা চিকন একটা বেটার আকৃতি টের পাইলাম. একটা কর্কশগোলার বেটা-বেটি একলগে কথা কইলে  যেমন স্বর হইতো অমন, রক্ত লাল চোখ দুইটা আমার দিকে অপলক চাইয়া.
'কেউ কয় টোকাই, কেউ কয় চোর তবে আমার কোনো নাম নাই. কিন্তু আমি মানুষ না দেইখা সাহস করতে পারসী.'
লোকমা করা ভাত না গিলে ওর দিকে তাকায় উত্তর দিলাম। ওই আকৃতিটা আমার দশহাত দূরে যেখানে দাঁড়ায় ছিল ঐখানে মাটিতে বইয়া পরে.
'জীর্ণশীর্ণ ছোট্ট বাচ্চা হইলেও তো তোমার চামড়া, মাংসল দেহ আর তাতে রক্ত আছে. তুমি কিভাবে মানুষ না!'
খাইতে আর পারলামনা, ঠোঙাটা পাশে রাইখা দিলাম, জীবনে কেউ আমার সাথে প্রথম কথা কইতে চাইলো তাই পেট খালি থাকলেও মনডা ভইরা গেলো.

'রক্ত মাংসে মানুষ হওয়া যায়না বাবা, সমাজে স্বীকৃতি লাগে মানুষ হইতে. আমার মা টোকাই ছিলেন মানুষ হওয়ার চেষ্টা করসিলেন এক লোকের হারানো টাকারবাগ দিয়া. হেরে মানুষ মারতে মারতে মাইরা ফেলাইসে ভুল বুইঝা. আমি মানুষ হইতে মরবার চাইনা, আমার মা'র দেয়া নাম ভুইলা গেসি, নিজেরে অমানুষ নাম দিসি। নিজেরে অমানুষ দাবি করি.'
'আমি এককালে মানুষ ছিলাম, নাম ছিল হরি, ব্রিটিশ আমলে এক জমিয়াদেরর সবচেয়ে প্রিয় গোলাম। আমিও মানুষ হইতে চেয়েছিলাম, চেয়েছিলাম সম্মান আর ভালোবাসা।'
'তোমার এই অবস্থা কেমনে হইলো।'

'জমিদার বাড়িতে আমার খুব নাম ডাক ছিল, প্রত্যেকটা কাজে হরি হরি করে সবাই পাগল, গ্রামের সবাই আমাকে খুব পছন্দ করতো। কারো সাথে আমার কোনো শত্রুতা ছিল না, আমি জীবনে একটা মাছি পর্যন্ত মারিনি গো। কিন্তু এই পৃথিবীতে হিংসা আর অহংকার মানুষ কে ছারে না। আমার সাথে কাজ করতো মহেশ, ওকে বন্ধু ভেবেছিলাম, কিন্তু ও ভাবতোনা। আমার বানানো রান্নায় বিষ ঢেলে আমার নাম অভিযোগ তুলে, আমাকে জমিদার বাড়ি থেকে বের করে দেয়া হয় গ্রামের লোকের অত্যাচার, অবহেলায় দুইদিন চলে যায়। শেষে আমি পেটের দায়ে আবার জমিদারের বাড়ি গেলাম তিনি আমাকে মাফ করলেন না, জানা গেলো দুইদিন ধরে তার স্ত্রী বিষক্রিয়ার কারণে ভুগছেন আর যখন আমি পৌছালাম তখন তিনি মারা গেলেন। আমাকে গ্রামবাসীর সামনে মৃত্যুদণ্ডের জন্য আদেশ করা হলো, আমি পালিয়ে গেলাম। দুঃখে কষ্টে গ্রাম থেকে পালিয়ে জঙ্গলে গেলাম। সেখানে একটা বয়স্ক লোক ছিলেন, যেই ভগবান আমাকে ছেড়ে দিয়েছেন তাকে আমি ছেড়ে দিলাম সেদিন তার কথায়। সে পেল তার যজ্ঞে আমার বলি আর আমি পেলাম শক্তি প্রতিশোধের। সবার আগে মহেশকে চিবিয়ে চিবিয়ে খেলাম, আমার মধ্যের মানুষ মরে জন্মনিলো একটা অমানুষ একটা রক্ত খেকো জানোয়ার। একেএকে গ্রামের সবাইকে খেতে শুরু করলাম, জমিদারককেও প্রতিশোধের আগুনে খেয়ে ফেললাম  । সেই রাতেই গ্রামের এক পন্ডিত গ্রামের আসেপাশে একটা পবিত্র রেখা টেনে দিয়ে আমাকে আটকে দিলো যেটা টপিকে তুমি এসেছো, প্রায় ১০০ বছর হয়ে গেছে।'
আমি আর পারলামনা বসে থাকতে হরির কথা শুনে, উঠে গিয়ে ওর কাছে গিয়ে ওকে জড়িয়ে ধরলাম।
'আমার মা, এভাবে আমাকে জড়িয়ে ধরতো যখন দুনিয়া আমারে কষ্ট দিতো। তোমার কোনো দোষ নাই হরি। তোমার সাথে যারা এমন করসে তারা অমানুষ ছিল, তুমি না।'

ওর শীতল দেহ,খোশখশে চামড়া, বিরাট বিরাট নখের হাত দিয়ে আমাকে জড়ায় ধরসে, ওরে বুঝাইতে বুঝাইতে আমি নিজেও কিছু বুঝলাম। আমি আমার খাবার নিয়ে যাইতে গেলাম, ও ঐখানেই বইয়া রইলো আর আমাকে ইশারায় এইখান থেকা খাওয়ান শেষ করে যাইতে কইলো, আমি তাই করলাম, আমার কেন যেনো মন বলসে আমাকে ও কিছু করবে না আর তাইই হইলো, আমি খাইলাম আর ততক্ষন চুপচাপ হরি আমারে দেখলো।  একটা আওয়াজ করলো না। আমি উঠে হাটা শুরু করসি এমন সময় আমারে ডাক দিলো।
'অমানুষ।'
আমি ফিরে তাকাইলাম। আলোর মধ্যে হরি দাঁড়ায় ছিল, ধোবদবে সাদা চামড়া, সুন্দর দেখতে,একটা মোচ, লম্বা চুল, ঠোটটা লাল টকটকে, লাল চোখ দিয়ে পানি পড়ছে তবে মুখে হাসি।

The mad woman in the attic.
Tired little flower,
gnawed on lion's tooth.
one day you'll be taller,
and fly over the static.
One day, the walls
would not hold you in at all.
But today the mold grows.
The foxes howl below your coop.
So for now, it's just the wishing stars,
And the lonely rays of the moon.
Unravel the patterns as you stare at the wallpaper.
The lines leading to the crossroads,
Of the brick road and the door.
On your right the hallways of the past
To the left the palace of future blooms.
Make your choice and either way
It's the king that grants your wisdom.
Sufferings of the ones before you,
Glimpses of inevitable doom.
Pray child, that you don't go
From the princess locked in the tower to the mad woman in the attic too soon.

runs.text: The Record and the Choice
The coin in your pocket, a planet in orbit, or the wheel of your childhood bicycle,if you take
the distance across that shape (its diameter) and around it (its circumference), then divide
that circumference by the diameter, you will undoubtedly land on π.
However, this is not a math lesson. π is more than just a string of decimals that your teacher
tells you to round to 3.14 on a random Tuesday. It is a storage of every piece of information
humanity has ever come across. With its infinite decimal numbers that never repeat into a
pattern, it is said that it holds every possible combination of numbers. Thus, somewhere in
the depths of the digits of π lies your birth date, your phone number, and the exact moment
of your greatest achievement. More surprisingly, if those numbers are converted into letters,
it holds the exact words of every lyric sung, every word ever uttered, and every book ever
written.
That would mean that the very words I am typing right now, or the thought I will form in a few
moments, already exist, sitting quietly in the infinite decimals of π.
Perhaps this means that the story of my life, your life, or simply what I am going to eat
tomorrow is all written in π. Now the question arises: if the map of my entire life was drawn
before I even drew my first breath, does that mean my choices aren’t really mine?
Okay wait, let me ask another one: this means that the next movie everyone is hyped about
and the score of tomorrow's match are all waiting quietly in π, even the lyrics of the song that
keeps popping up on your "For You" page every other day. Why write the script anyway, or
why spend so much time thinking about the perfect words for the article that you will have to
publish tomorrow?
I know I am getting a bit out of hand, because although this information exists, it certainly
does not in the first 100,000 digits of π. And since it is infinite, you can’t really tell where it
exists. However, as technology emerges and advances, I assume it won't be very difficult to
continue calculating many digits of π and thus find such information.
Now, even if finding it is impossible, let us take a hypothetical situation where we know all the
digits of π. This would mean that somewhere in there is every scrap of information you could
possibly find. Does this mean that my whole life isn’t really mine, or maybe I shouldn’t even
bother writing this article, because somewhere in the digits of π, there is everything I will ever
think, say, or do,so... what even is the point?
The answer lies in the fact that a record of what will happen is not the force or action that
makes it happen. In the infinite digits of π. There are also every other variation of my life: one
where I fail the test, one where I skip breakfast, and one where a single digit of my phone
number is altered. Therefore, even if a supercomputer does find all the digits of π, I wouldn’t
know whether a given sequence is my actual life or just a false variant.
If I choose to study today and get good marks on my test, that specific reality exists in the
digits of π. But if I choose not to study and fail, that outcome is also sitting somewhere in π.
The record exists because I choose it, not the other way around.

the featureless grey dust.

particular telescope back home in Moscow. Some anomalous signal or some such. But

he begins,

happened?!

being hunted for sport. Halfway there, the operator stops responding. A second later, the
music cuts off.

plans to reason his way out of this. “
Alright, this thing is probably an extraterrestrial; that’s

that unbearable weight settling in on his chest once more, before-

definitely can’t talk to it. He decides his only hope now is to attempt to outrun the
Lovecraftian nightmare. He isn’t very optimistic about his prospects, but what other choice

site.

fast

he’s in the rover, driving

title: The Others
author: Fahmiah Fahreen

runs.text: I. The oil pastels
Squeezed into the plastic box, they stay there, behind the sheaf of papers, cracked files and old books.
Some tall and proud despite fading colors, some stubbed and wedged painfully at the feet of others,
some with their covers peeling and adorned with a mass of networking scribbles, and others
fairly…alright, they huddle there in the dark like refugees in a camp.
They’ve been like this for a fairly long time, waiting for the sudden bursts of instances where they sensed a
slant of light over their plastic home, felt the wretched walls before them being stirred and moved over to
the side as the plastic box was pulled out.
For the first time in a while, the lid would be turned and they’d see light, and a wonderful view of the
cracked ceiling above. They would be selected to show themselves off on a thin sheet of paper, a task they
completed very eagerly indeed. And even as they’re placed back into the dark, the excitement and utter
pride of the ones who were selected would provide enough fuel for life for the days to come.
And so they sit there, more or less patient, for the only one who had the power to grant them this long
awaited momentary freedom. The only one who could crack the rigid walls before them and let them see
light.
So they wait, and they wait for her.
How much longer?
II. The plastic cup
Holding on to the arm of the metal stand, it watches as the next batch is taken to the sink.
There’s plates, pans, saucers and bowls, alongside glasses and cups just like itself, waiting their turn to be
doused in the cold water. Some of the cups send fleeting glances of pity, while others remain rigid, their
backs turned to it.
It remembered back when it used to be part of this batch, participating in merry clacks, clitters and thuds
into the bustling conversations that took place at the sink. Everyone had complaints about their use: being
too rough, using too much oil, using too less, being ruthlessly stashed into the rack, jumbled up with others.
It itself never took part in this, it never had to. It liked the touch of the small, warm fingers of its user curling
around its handle, the sloshing of water to dissolve the orange juice powder at its bottom, the soft sips, the
noisy ones with the following burst of cheeky laughter, the unicorn and barbie stickers smothered over its
surface.
For some time now, though, it’s been hanging from the rack, relieved of its duties. This happened sometimes
of course, for a whole month once, but she always returned, sometimes bringing a new sticker to take its
place on the pale orange surface.
Yes, that must be the case, it thought as it watched the water gurgling over the others at the sink.
Yes, that’s it.
Then why wasn’t it taken to the sink?
And what was this throb it felt, as if something else had happened?
III. The schoolbag
Stashed under the table, it counted footsteps. Footsteps of the people coming into the room, going out.1, 2,
Just 14 footsteps today. From three different people. Far too less. It could be wrong. The lights barely
came on at night, and it had to rely on sound. During the day, it seemed to be just the maid, dragging the
broom behind her. It could be wrong. It probably was. It felt more tired now, slumping here against the
dimness. Fully packed, it felt the load of the books and copies inside itself, neatly slotted according to
period, the pencil case reigning in its separate pocket. The tiffin box was there too, for a while, until it was
taken out a while ago, leaving the water bottle behind. It would be a Tuesday, then, according to the
arrangement of the books.
Then why weren’t they taken out?

runs.text: Liar
H
e loved poetry
but it was not in his destiny
He was enrolled in medical school
and alas! He felt like a fool.
He thought that it was fine,
to just bite and lie.
Stethoscope stifled him
scalpel bled his soul.
He could not survive it
He endured so.
He thought that it was fine,
to just smile and lie.
He considered his other half
who could never be enough
And pretending is poisonous
slowly punishing their love.
He thought that it was fine,
to just sigh and lie.
His melancholy maimed him
As well willing to let his child dream
Because he knows what it costs to lie
when you have borrowed your wings to fly.

title: The Tale of The Mediterranean
author: Naziba Zahin

runs.text: The Tale of The Mediterranean
People love that word. Illegal. Illegal immigrant. Illegal border. Illegal boat. They say it with
clean mouths, in clean rooms, over clean water. Nobody says illegal hunger. Nobody says
illegal poverty. Nobody says illegal childhood without food.
The sea doesn’t care about any of that. It just swallows.
Salt water burns my throat. Behind me, a child is choking—crying, maybe praying. It smells
like vomit and sweat and fear. The sky is too beautiful tonight. Stars everywhere, silent, far
away. The sea glitters even while it kills. I hate how beautiful it looks.
The stars make me think of her.
I’m back in that government hospital. Stained walls. A fan creaking like it might fall. Patients,
nurses, pain. Then she cried, and none of it mattered. I held her like she was glass. I
promised her safety. I had no right to promise that. She wrapped her fingers around mine
and I felt ashamed. When she smiled the first time, I thought I’d seen heaven.
I took the bracelet home from the hospital. It’s been in my wallet since. It’s wet now. I keep
touching it.
After she was born, I worked and counted money. Somehow it was never enough. Her
clothes grew smaller, and I kept telling myself things would get better. They didn’t. I sold my
land. I sold my mother’s jewelry. I can still see the empty box. I sold my dignity piece by
piece until all I had left was this journey. I paid for a seat on a boat that shouldn’t be floating.
It’s full of men like me. Not criminals. Not monsters. Just fathers who ran out of options.
The world loves a sacrifice story. Noble. Beautiful. Make a movie about it. But when we
actually do it—when we actually risk our lives—they call us illegal. They want our sacrifice to
stay poetic. Not real.
The boat rocks. Someone screams. Someone prays. Someone throws up. The smell of
death gets stronger. Like death is already here, sitting with us, waiting.
I count my days. Maybe hours. I keep thinking about her face. I can’t remember the exact
sound of her laugh anymore. That scares me more than the waves. I’m scared I’ll die without
remembering her right. I’m scared my love won’t be enough to keep her safe. I’m scared I’ll
get to Europe and still fail her.
The sea doesn’t answer that either.
If I live, maybe she’ll grow up where she doesn’t know hunger. She’ll learn a language I can’t
speak. Wear clothes I can’t afford. Laugh at things I’ll never understand. And maybe one day
she’ll forget me. Let her. If she sleeps warm, if she eats, if she grows up without fear, I won’t
ask for anything more.
Another wave hits.
I close my eyes. I see her. Her fingers around mine. Her first smile. The warmth of her
against my chest. I wish I could hold her one more time. The water rises. I try to hear her
laugh, but all I hear is the sea.
Will she remember me?
Then it goes dark.
The tale of the Mediterranean will go on...
I just hope she knows I tried.

runs.text: Music and the sound of classics by
Nazrul
leak through the grand doors of
the theater reaching the ears of Usha. She hums along, the melodies being
ingrained into her head while her small hands sweep away the torn up
tickets in the hall. Usha always loved singing, so this was perfect for her.
Sometimes, she'd imagine herself on those stages. Sparkly
saree
, her long
hair tied into an intricate braid laced with her favorite flowers, and her
brother, Mahin in the crowd. People would line up to hear her sing! The
theater would be booming-
A tap on her shoulder pulls her out of the daydreams behind her eyelids.
Oh uncle, kichu lagbe?”
(Oh uncle, do you need something?)
“Na mamoni, kintu tor shathe ektu kotha chilo.” (No sweetheart, but I need
to talk to you about something.)
“Ki hoyeche ebar? Abar ki Mitur shift amake bhorte Hobe? Shomoshha nai
ami-” (What happened this time? Do I need to cover Mitu’s shift again?
That's no problem, I can-)
“Na, na. Ektu shun maa, upor theke budget katse, amader onek jonke
chere dite hochhe arki…” (No,no listen to me sweetheart, upper
management made budget cuts, we're having to lay off a lot of people…)
Usha being only eighteen almost nineteen, doesn't quite understand the
connotations. Only when her manager explicitly tells her she's fired, does
her mind comprehend the situation. Dread washes over her when she
leaves the theater. It's peak business hours for the street stalls that cover
Dhaka in the scent of reused oil and unhealthy junk food. Schoolboys
laughing among themselves, people getting off work. Usha envies them.
Why does everyone have it so much easier than her? Why does she have
to do so much? And even then she gets fired, it's like she's the ultimate
loser. The only thing in this world the street lamps don't shine their light
down onto.
No, it's fine, she's fine. She'll find another job tomorrow, it'll be okay. Mahin
is waiting, she needs to go home.
Mahin? Mahin!”(Mahin? Mahin!)
The house is quiet, too quiet. Usha throws back her head in annoyance
and moves to the kitchen. Empty cupboards, empty jars, she finds just
enough lentils to make one last serving of Khichuri. The sound of water
inconsistently running from the tap fills the tiny structure. It's the last thing
Usha and Mahin’s parents left them. Their funeral was extremely
overwhelming for Usha. She remembers holding Mahin and not being able
to explain to him what's going on. Her memories of that day are interrupted
by the front door slowly creaking open. Her voice echoes through the
apartment.
“Mahin! Kothai chili tui? Edik ai!” (Mahin! Where were you? Come here!)
Mahin’s sneaky entrance is a failure. He huffs in disappointment and walks
to the kitchen, his head hanging while he hides his hands behind his back.
“Apu.. Emni ektu khelchilam Riyander shathe..”(Apu.. I was just playing
with Riyan and the others..)
“Khelle khelbi, shomoi moto ashte ki shomoshha??”(If you want to play, you
can play but what's the issue with coming home in time???)
She turns
around to scold him further, only to be met by his shirt, turning damper by
the second from his dripping wet hair. Mahin prepares for the explosion, he
counts in his head,
“Tui abar oi pukur e dubte gechish??? Kotobar toke bolechi ami tui e
amake bol. Oi pukure jabi na, otar kacheo jabi na emonki, ota niye chintao
korbi na tui! Beche thakte gaye lage ki? Ki ar bolbo toke…”(You went to go
drown in that pond again??? How many times have I told you, you tell me.
Don't go to that pond, don't go near that pond in fact, don't even think about
that pond! Does it bother you to stay alive? What can I even say…)
Usha hates that pond. It's disgustingly dirty, the water murkier than even
the drains scattered across this city. God knows what creatures lurk in
there. But the neighborhood kids seem to that bowl of bacteria as a
goldmine of enjoyment.
Mahin's eyes well up with fat, sparkly tears
“Kintu kichu hoi na toh, kichu
hobeo na. Tumi emni emni amake boka dao.” (But nothing happened
though, nothing's gonna happen. You scold me for no reason at all)
Usha’s eyes soften. She leans down and moves his wet hair away from his
forehead, she mumbles out an apology.
“Apur bhoi lage, Mahin. Achha, I'm sorry, holo? Asho, chul ta muche di.”
(Apu gets scared, Mahin. Alright, I'm sorry, okay? Come, let me dry your
hair.)
Mahin tells her about all of his superhero adventures of the day while his
hair gets dried by that worn out, blue towel. Usha smiles hearing, playing
along with his heroic stories, praising him for his bravery. The pressure
cooker whistles loudly, announcing to the world the Khichuri is done. Mahin
covers his little ears, annoyed by the noise. He eats the Khichuri, only after
Usha convinces him she ate at the theater.
Mahin gets into bed and begs for Usha to sing him a lullaby, as he does
every single night. Mahin simply won't sleep without it, so she obliges. He
smiles through the first, refusing to close his eyes, the second brings out a
soft yawn, while the third closes his eyes and lulls him into his dreams.
Usha lays down next to him. She can't bring herself to close her eyes. She
tells herself she'll be fine, everything will be fine. There's countless jobs in
the world, she'll do anything, she has to do anything. That realization keeps
her staring at the ceiling until the chickens start calling. It's alright, she's
gone without sleep before. She fixes Mahin's breakfast, last night's
leftovers. There's nothing else. It actually motivates her. She should get out
nice and early so she can find a job and start immediately. So that's exactly
what she does. She closes the front door, careful not to make a peep or a
certain black haired child will come running to wish his older sister
goodbye.
The street lights have been on for hours, but they don't highlight Usha’s joy.
Because it isn't there. 16 places. She's been to 16 places and yet, no one
wanted to employ her. They tell her she's too young, too inexperienced,
and a plethora of other faults. All the hope she had when she shut the front
door has disappeared from her form, as a deflated sunflower when the sun
must rise on the other side. She can barely breathe from fear, she has no
idea how her feet are carrying her through the empty streets of Dhaka. Her
blurry eyes are fixed on the ground. The electricity bill, the water bill,
groceries, how is she going to pay for anything? What is she going to do?
What is she going to tell Mahin?
Wait, this neighborhood, it's the one before Usha’s. It has that night guard.
He never can mind his own business. Always pestering Usha about her

It was back in 2013, when I was in class four that I first met Babul sir. He was my Islamic studies teacher. I remember the first time he saw me, and how he never looked away, not until he was already in his seat, and one of my classmates was asking him what he’d teach us today. Babul sir ignored him entirely. His very first words were, “We have a new beauty in our class!”
I instantly knew who he was talking about, not just me, but everyone present. I was the new student after all. Did his compliment make me feel flustered and shy? No.
I was unnerved.

Not because all attention was on me then, but because of the look in Babul sir’s eyes. Something about the way he watched his new student felt primal and unprofessional. The way his eyes never left me even as he asked me to stand up and introduce myself despite the fact that I had already done so in the first period, and the way his sleazy eyes scanned my every move. It was… disgusting.

Now, here I was, five years later, watching the man as he exited the administration building, or more like the principal’s office after receiving his expulsion notice. With his head bowed, he avoided eye contact and scurried out like a little sewer rat. But this time, my eyes never left him.

Apparently, some students from junior classes had reported him for sexual assault, not one or two, but many, and when the complaints kept piling up, they decided it was time to let this long-standing faculty member go, that is if they wanted to protect the school’s image. I knew those girls. They were in fourth grade, same as when I was. Some of them had sisters in my class, which was why news travelled quickly to me. Turns out, Babul sir had become quite bold over the years.

From watching female students and unnerving them, he had moved on to even touching them, holding hands, placing them on his lap, and what not. All in the name of ‘Teacherly affection.” Or sometimes, “Fatherly figure”. I didn’t know father’s affections were supposed to be this uncomfortable.

The little girls who filed the complaints came rushing to our class to inform their sisters about the good news, and I remember the joy in their faces. The feeling of justice being served, and the pride that took over them at the notion that it was them who took the first step. All I could do was smile and keep my silence. Like I always have.

They had finally brought an end to years of little girls getting assaulted, making sure they were the last. But… in order to do that, they had to fall victim to him first. Had I spoken up all those years ago, could I have saved them from witnessing what I did? And all those that came before them? If I had, would things have been different for them?
But, who would have believed me?
“Babul sir? Yeah, I know him. He teaches Islamic studies to me too. What about him?”
“I... I don’t know. He makes me feel very uncomfortable in class.”
“How so?”
“H-He… he’s always… staring at me.”
“That’s all?”
“I-I k-know it doesn’t sound much but… how do I explain? I-It’s like… the way he stares-”
“Every teacher stares at a student when they are asking them something.”
“Yeah I know b-but, it’s not just when he’s asking m-”
“Good Lord Mariam! He teaches us in eighth grade too! And he’s as normal as everyone else!”
“W-What…”

“Seriously, Mariam. Stop making a good man sound like such a pervert! All he did was just look at you like any other student! Also, maybe because you are new! If he was a bad man, why’s he so good to us?”

I don’t know, Hajera. Maybe because it was kids that he targeted and not older children, because they were easy to manipulate. And I was a new student only for a few days, not for the whole year. Why then did his eyes roam over every inch of my body for the whole year that he taught us?

Is that why nobody spoke up for all these years? Because the kids were easily manipulated? Perhaps the only reason why these little girls knew what he was doing was wrong because of their older sisters who warned them of the sort of man he was. Because we all saw how he watched me, and no part of it was normal.
And I did not get manipulated to believe it was normal. For I had already experienced this years ago.
Dear reader, if you have read this far, there’s a question I’d like to ask you.
Have you ever met a woman, girl, or child that has never experienced being touched without consent?

He was a distant relative of mom. He’d come by our house every so often like he was best buddies with my mom while in reality they were hardly blood related. But I should have known, he wasn’t coming to see mom or chatting with dad. He was here for the little children.
He was here for Safiya and me.

Safiya was nine, I was seven, but I remember him all too well. My memories from my childhood are slowly turning foggy like they are no longer mine, but Hasib I would always remember. He was the first person to teach me what inappropriate touch meant.

The first day he came, mom dressed me up in a skirt and shirt. It was very pretty, with red polka dots that had shimmer on them. I liked that dress a lot. Like every guest, he pretended to dot on the two little children of the house, offer gifts and even money, pick us up and lift us in the air as we giggled. That should have been it. It was for every other guest. But for Hasib, he was still not finished. After all, he had offered us gifts and money, he needed his worth.
He’d sit back on his chair, place Safiya or I in his lap, lift up our shirts and press his rough, calloused hands against our soft tummy’s. Just like that.

He’d sit there for hours, the heat from his body and hands pressing against our little frames, while his hands stayed under our shirts for purposes I couldn’t comprehend. I didn’t know. I didn’t even know this was wrong. Nobody told me it was. Hasib sat there with me between his legs, his hands under my shirt, and everybody pretended it was not happening, or it was normal. So how was a little child of seven supposed to say she felt wronged?
How was she supposed to tell she didn’t like what was happening, when the adults around her made no noise about it?

I was used to guests pecking me on the cheek as a show of affection for a little child. Hasib would do something else. He’d pull me flat against his chest, press kisses down my nape, and sometimes even my shoulders. It was ticklish, and it was horrifying. Trying to wiggle my way out of his lap wasn’t possible, in case I woke something else up.
I didn’t even know I could wake something else up.

I was seven, but when he left, I found myself breathing like I had been holding myself back from it. When he’d come back, it felt like being pulled under water so my lungs could fill with water and I’d suffocate. I was seven.
Dear reader, here’s my second question. Does reading this make you uncomfortable? Does it make you want to put it down and pretend you never read it?

At a school function, Hajera insisted I wear the skirt and shirt with red shimmery polka dots, since I liked it the most and looked the prettiest. I agreed with a smile. And then proceeded to mistakenly spill juice over it.
During a visit to the hospital for mom, I accompanied her, and she dressed me in that dress again. I agreed with a smile. And then proceeded to vomit on it during the bus ride.

The following year, mom was donating clothes that no longer fit us or we didn’t like anymore. The polka dot dress was the first to go. It shocked everyone since the dress was my favorite, and it still fit. But it had to go. I could not tell them that the dress still smelt like Hasib even after I spilled juice on it, or vomited, or had it washed a thousand times. I could not tell them that the texture of it reminded me of his unwanted touch, of his rough hands pressed against my toddler skin. I could not tell them it has not been my favorite for a long time now. I just said I no longer liked it, and it had to go. Nobody complained.

Hasib’s visit only lasted a year, but the times he came that year were enough to scar my memory for life, to the point I had built a defensive wall around me for a lifetime. No longer can I look a male in the eyes, nor can I hear them when they talk or address me, and the worst of all, stand their touch. No matter who it is. Everything just reminds me of those calloused hands pressing against me.

Which is why it was easier for me to recognize the look in Babul sir’s eyes the moment they fell on me and never left. I had come to build a habit of recognizing a certain type of person, and I’m surprised I wasn’t wrong. Babul sir proved to be exactly what my consciousness had feared- a pedophile like Hasib.

I had never spoken about this to anyone, nor has anyone ever asked. Which makes me wonder, just how many more of us are out there, our stories buried between the folds of our trauma, alive, but never released? Surviving, but never shared to the public? Why? Because it is too grotesque to read? Too shameful to share? But not shameful enough to avoid committing? Why does it become shameful when the prey shares the experience, but not shameful when the predator commits it?
So dear reader, here is my third question to you. When you speak about dark romance just being fictional and nothing to do with reality, which part are you speaking about?
The part where his eyes scan all over your body?
The part where his rough, calloused hands grip you to make you immobile?
The part where the heat from his body takes over your tiny frame?
The touch of his rough skin against your soft ones?
The part where he forcefully makes you sit on his lap?
Kisses your nape and shoulders?
Grinds against you?
Makes you wake up his beast?
Which part is fictional? Because to me this sounds like the horrifying reality of a victim of sexual assault. So… which part of this ‘darkness’ is supposed to be ‘romantic’?
Since when did abuse and assault get involved with romance?

How easy it is to write a novella about romanticizing assault and naming it love without having to witness it in reality. Because in reality, it’s never romantic. It’s never love. It’s a horror movie where your consent is thrown out the window, your please fall to deaf ears, and your existence becomes similar to a still furniture.
You are no longer a living being.
When abuse is packaged as romance, the narrative framing itself can turn abusive behavior into something desirable, acceptable, or even proof of love.
But yes. Let’s call it romance. And let’s normalize reading it to young children so they get silenced even more. So, they no longer have the ability to discern between assault and affection.

My classmates had already gone home, while I waited for my brother to come pick me up. The campus was almost empty. And by the looks of it, Babul sir must have waited till it was so he did not have to face a crowd while leaving.

This time, I watched him like he’d watched me that whole year, like a hawk hungry for its prey. I watched him at his lowest, at his most vulnerable, read his body language and how exposed he felt. And I enjoyed it a lot. Just like he enjoyed watching young girls all this time.

I may have not been able to sack this man, I may never be able to expose Hasib or men like him. Because the society I come from condemns people like me more than it condemns people like Hasib and Babul. But I will not judge another like me either.

I will not ask her if she was making things up, or if she was dressed appropriately, or if she had looked at him first to give him that attention. I will not ask her if she was out late, or if she started it.
All she needs to tell me is she didn’t want it. And that’s enough.

title: Fish tank
author: Tinkori

runs.text: The fish tank is tiny and cramped and the exterior of it is stained an ugly shade of brown that can only be accumulated through years of neglected water stains. In it, a tiny blue fish swims to and fro. Thrashing its little fins and tail in the murky water from one corner to another as if it has anywhere else to be other than in the tiny cave settled over the small pebbles or under the poor plastic imitation of seaweeds.

In front of it, the girl stands with her hands inside her pockets. The dim light overhead does nothing to illuminate the emptiness that surrounds the vinyl floorings and walls with its ripped wallpapers and greenish mold emerging on the ceilings. The girl stares unblinkingly at the tank for a while. The blue fish butts its head once, twice into the tiny hole of the cave and swims away, (something clearly put there far before the fish had grown to its current size) returning to its sisyphean form of swimming in endless circles.

The girl doesn't look at the other fishes for as long, at the lonely guppies, at the twin betta fishes in the same tank, at the dull cardinal tetras or the other myriad of fishes ‘sleeping’ with their bellies up in their equally sad cramped aquariums and pebbled cages.
The fish she wanted to see isn't here.

The speakers whir a soft tune, something pitchy and faraway like a sirencall. It cracks here and there and gives a distorted effect to the already creepy music. She fishes her phone out of the ratty messenger bag slung across her shoulders and clicks a picture.
The resulting flash spooks the tiny fish and it rushes to resume its fruitless attempt at squeezing into the hide.
A ping cracks the haunting stillness of the place. It's Hope, replying to whatever they were talking about yesterday with a bunch of crying emoticons.
Lia only shares the picture of the tank in reply.
‘It’s not an aquarium. It's a pet store. They lied on the website.’
The typing bubble appears and disappears. Her fingers hover over the screen as she waits. The bubble disappears once more. Lia opens the call logs.
No new missed calls.
A new notification ping.
Hope: Lol.

Lia sighs and turns her phone off, intending to go back to the blue fish but before she can, the music suddenly stops and moves on to a commercial, something cheery and dull as she is interrupted by the stout shop owner materializing right behind her.
“Would you like to buy the fish, miss?”

On the way back home, the streets are emptier than usual. The recent rain has polished the pavements and the occasional car driving by or the flickering street lights reflect off of the asphalt like a strange canvas from another world. Sometimes, Lia thinks she's stuck in a painting. Unmoving and unreal. Forever tied to the same place as the world outside flashes and honks by.
She checks her pockets again for her student ID, her pass to one more year of free bus rides before she has to bite the bullet and learn how to drive for herself.

Her boots squelch as she walks up to the town bridge and takes another look at her phone. It's a while till the 11:30 bus. The night feels colder now, with the occasional drizzle still dampening Lia's hair.
A flash of memory. A different sort of cold. Piercing and sharp and all encompassing. Traveling down the throat and towards the-

A car passes by with a loud honk. Lia looks down at the water, the dark mass off it crashing against the beams of the bridge in a sort of insistent manner. As if trying to knock it over little by little.
She hasn't been here since the last time, on a similar night perhaps that feels like it was decades ago; feels as if it were yesterday.

The cold is seeping through her shirt now. Lia doesn't untie her hoodie from where it hangs at her waist to wrap it around herself. She stares at the minute waves, imagines the ripple of water lapping at her feet, her waist and her cheeks. The sharp sting of it making her teeth clatter, the blinding pain, the comforting pressure.
Had it not felt like an embrace?

Lia shakes her head. Once. Twice. And then again. She focuses on the sharp edges of her student ID, wearing down from the same ritual. Useless now other than for getting free rides and the occasional checks. Dulling just like the days once more. She thinks back to the papercut she had gotten writing the letter that day, eyes blurring and restricting her view of her own words.
Another shake. Another swipe down the edges.

Lia forces her mind back to the Cherry Barbs, thinks back to her mothers voice telling her how they swim in groups. A story from another life when she and Lia's father had still been together, when she had fallen asleep reading her ‘The rainbow fish’ and Lia had cuddled under her heavy arms; sighing like a content cat under the warmth.
At three years old Lia had thought the story to be dreadful. Lia still does not know how the story ends.
She imagines how it would've ended, imagines the Cherry barb’s shiny scales skirting beneath the murky waves of the city river, sticking close against the ruthless current.

title: What Remains When The Room Empties
author: Raisa Uddin

runs.text: The morning is spent putting on our faces, the afternoon drifts as we perform our parts, and the
night falls over as we think which of the casts was actually us.
My footsteps were light as they approached the doorstep to my room, my very own sanctuary.
The doorknob twists under my hand. The door clicks shut behind, leaving just me. My bag falls
onto the floor, heavy with textbooks and the unspoken weight of the afternoon. The room is a
stark contrast to the echoes that linger in my mind. A tension I did not know I was carrying
leaves my shoulders. My face relaxes, dropping its forced choreography.
Behind the closed door, an ambient hum settles, yet the most raucous sound was the lingering
noise of the day inside my head. It hovers over me as though it were the sky that shrouds my
world. The clever responses I did not mean, the polite laughs at jokes that were hardly funny,
the careful, maintained posture; all seem to dissolve in the deafening silence. I seem to have
lost count of how many of me exist in a single body. How come nothing is easy when I find so
many of me? Outside this very closed door, I find myself responsive, ready to take over, and
composed like I'm following a script, but here, perhaps, there is no script to follow.
Earlier this afternoon, I was nodding attentively as each lesson progressed, later I stood in the
crowded hallway, mixing into the crowd ever so seamlessly. The image of the accommodating
friend, polite listener, diligent peer, all felt so natural at that moment. Now, everything seems
ridiculous. With a sharp exhale, I pull my knees to my chest as I burrow my head beneath. My
shoulders that felt so heavy, sink as my breath slows down to a steady hum, and the heart
beating against the cage inside my chest beats rhythmically. For eight hours or more, I was but
a mosaic of expectations, constructed from what others wanted me to be.Thinking back, the
task feels exhausting, but the harsh reality tells me it is my daily routine. Was I always like this?
When did I resort to this?
I try to trace back past the polished behavior, and rehearsed speeches, hoping to find a time
when words could flow out easily without having to be filtered through a sieve first. Then again,
will that answer the questions that keep coming back?
People play their parts like they know what should be shown, and perhaps that is what I do too.
The world really is just a stage with us being the actors. Wouldn't you agree? I lift my head with
ease as if the heavy weight of what it holds is nothing. My eyes stare blankly at the wall ahead. I
feel like an endless void. Who am I really? The identities that I unknowingly created are like
costumes hung at the back of the closet, waiting to be worn. Realization dawns upon the
entirety of myself in this small room. Tomorrow, when the sun rises and the birds begin their soft
chirp, this process will repeat. My shoulders will straighten, my lips will curve into a smile that
does not fully reach my eyes, and the whole puzzle will piece itself together accordingly. Being
stuck in this miserable loop is the truth of me living. I wonder if the actor that graces the day will
ever meet the one that lives in the dark. In the quiet I am left with the question of what actually
remains at the end of the day.

runs.text: The Revival
I wake up to the brazen sound of my alarm clock feeling like a soulless pit of lost potential
again. I sit up and grab my phone to open my socials and end up doom-scrolling for an hour,
smiling at others happiness while crying at others loss. I look at the time, its 11 a.m. Realizing
how much time I’ve wasted, a surge of venomous guilt makes me hate myself for a second.
Technology has given us far more than we can ever imagine, but like a quiet midnight thief, it
has taken a lot from us as well. As I fight off the thought that the days of my life are being
reduced to nothing as I live vicariously through others online, I get the idea of walking around
my new neighbourhood. I get up and start getting ready to go outside.
As I step outside, the wind welcomes me with a warm hug. It’s hot outside but not the
irritating kind. The kind that only exists during the month of Chaitra; remnants of a childhood
memory. The same childhood in which I used to paint and write stories at my leisure. Those
pastimes have now escaped me like this intangible spring wind. Nowadays, my only
recreation’s my phone.
I walk not knowing where my legs will take me. Ahead of me, I see a woman sitting alone on a
bench. I walk towards her. Without hesitation, I sit beside her, only a few inches gap between
us. And a few words unsaid until we have a conversation. Looking at her, I realize she’s
probably in her mid-sixties. She looks at me and smiles, she has a genuine smile and bright
eyes. Eyes that never age, in a peculiar way she’s younger than me. I think she could tell I lack
the spirit she prides herself with because she starts speaking to me. “Do you live nearby?”
she asks. “Yes, I moved in recently, haven’t looked around the neighbourhood yet,” I reply
solemnly. Hearing this, her eyes light up as she grabs me by my hand and stands up.
Surprised, I let out a quiet gasp and stand up with her. She starts walking with my hand in
hers as I try to keep up with her. “Where are you taking me?” I ask stupefied. She says,
almost with religious conviction,
“Something sweet about pleasantries,
About incoherent smiles or tricks.
Or mistaken eye contacts-
Looking into each other’s ‘guise.
Something scary about familiarity,
Like the unnoticed bland taste of life; the loop of a burning sun and a peeking moon.
That love might just be fleeting moments worth embracing;
Worth embracing the colours that suffuse our life.
Something electric about the voracity of our minds words; the Charybdis of our thoughts.
Pour your potable words over the earth and let it shape a path for you.
Give me a taste of your words and I’ll give you a taste of mine.”
I stop in my tracks trying to soak in her words. Understanding, she stands by me as the
midday sun glares down at us. I feel the warmth of her soul and the comforting hand of hope
on my shoulder. “Will you go with me?” she asks softly. “Take me with you,” I say without
hesitation. The old woman takes me to a rundown building with a massive nameplate at the
front. It says, “Manobotar Ovayaronno” -the Sanctuary of Humanity. At its entrance the
guard let us enter only after we gave him our phones. I feel vulnerable without my phone but
it’s also liberating. The old woman leads me into a big room with grey walls, red curtains,
windows and a few antique wooden chairs. Slowly, many people start filling in the empty
seats around us. A man appears before us and asks us who wants to go first. Confused, I look
around for answers but everyone looks ahead attentively. A girl goes to the front. She starts
reciting:
“Art is a drop of water that you yearn for in deserts,
It’s grief masked by melancholy,
It’s the chorus of laughter on the streets,
The dimmed light of shops existing from long before me,
The bending curves of mother earth,
The filial banyan trees’ bondage with each root,
Art is the first sounds a child learns to make,
It’s the journey from dusk till dawn by trains undestined,
A forgiving smile of the moon,
Or scandalous winks by night stars,
it’s the light you see with your eyes shut before the raging sun,
Art is blind and forgiving.
Art is provoking and humane.
Art lends us the sensations of life.”
Everyone claps when she finishes. The old woman casts a sideways smile at me. I can’t help
but smile back. “That was beautiful,” I whisper to her. One after another, people recite the
poems they wrote. Their words reverberating among us like an echo.
I realize that this is what’s been missing in my life- this exchange of words, of art, of
humanity replacing digital monotony. Art is the blood coursing through our veins. Art
distinguishes between mankind and mechanoids. The death of art is the death of humanity.
I feel the passion emanating from every one and can’t help but fall in love. I glance at the
old woman and suddenly it occurs to me how much of an impact she’s made on me with
such a short encounter. But, that’s all it takes sometimes- an exchange of a few words
between souls.
The concrete wall is no more itself,
It carries the vitality of being spotted by elusive colours;
Colours that prove existence.
I gained back my soul today.

As I fight off the thought that the days of my life are being reduced to nothing as I live vicariously through others online, I get the idea of walking around my new neighbourhood. I get up and start getting ready to go outside.

As I step outside, the wind welcomes me with a warm hug. It’s hot outside but not the irritating kind. The kind that only exists during the month of Chaitra; remnants of a childhood memory. The same childhood in which I used to paint and write stories at my leisure. Those pastimes have now escaped me like this intangible spring wind. Nowadays, my only recreation’s my phone.

I walk not knowing where my legs will take me. Ahead of me, I see a woman sitting alone on a bench. I walk towards her. Without hesitation, I sit beside her, only a few inches gap between us. And a few words unsaid until we have a conversation. Looking at her, I realize she’s probably in her mid-sixties. She looks at me and smiles, she has a genuine smile and bright eyes. Eyes that never age, in a peculiar way she’s younger than me. I think she could tell I lack the spirit she prides herself with because she starts speaking to me. “Do you live nearby?” she asks. “Yes, I moved in recently, haven’t looked around the neighbourhood yet,” I reply solemnly. Hearing this, her eyes light up as she grabs me by my hand and stands up. Surprised, I let out a quiet gasp and stand up with her. She starts walking with my hand in hers as I try to keep up with her. “Where are you taking me?” I ask stupefied. She says, almost with religious conviction, “Something sweet about pleasantries, About incoherent smiles or tricks. Or mistaken eye contacts- Looking into each other’s ‘guise. Something scary about familiarity, Like the unnoticed bland taste of life; the loop of a burning sun and a peeking moon. That love might just be fleeting moments worth embracing; Worth embracing the colours that suffuse our life.

Something electric about the voracity of our minds words; the Charybdis of our thoughts. Pour your potable words over the earth and let it shape a path for you. Give me a taste of your words and I’ll give you a taste of mine.”

I stop in my tracks trying to soak in her words. Understanding, she stands by me as the midday sun glares down at us. I feel the warmth of her soul and the comforting hand of hope on my shoulder. “Will you go with me?” she asks softly. “Take me with you,” I say without hesitation. The old woman takes me to a rundown building with a massive nameplate at the front. It says, “Manobotar Ovayaronno” -the Sanctuary of Humanity. At its entrance the guard let us enter only after we gave him our phones. I feel vulnerable without my phone but it’s also liberating. The old woman leads me into a big room with grey walls, red curtains, windows and a few antique wooden chairs. Slowly, many people start filling in the empty seats around us. A man appears before us and asks us who wants to go first. Confused, I look around for answers but everyone looks ahead attentively. A girl goes to the front. She starts reciting: “Art is a drop of water that you yearn for in deserts, It’s grief masked by melancholy, It’s the chorus of laughter on the streets, The dimmed light of shops existing from long before me, The bending curves of mother earth, The filial banyan trees’ bondage with each root, Art is the first sounds a child learns to make, It’s the journey from dusk till dawn by trains undestined, A forgiving smile of the moon, Or scandalous winks by night stars, it’s the light you see with your eyes shut before the raging sun, Art is blind and forgiving. Art is provoking and humane. Art lends us the sensations of life.” Everyone claps when she finishes. The old woman casts a sideways smile at me. I can’t help but smile back. “That was beautiful,” I whisper to her. One after another, people recite the poems they wrote. Their words reverberating among us like an echo.

I realize that this is what’s been missing in my life- this exchange of words, of art, of humanity replacing digital monotony. Art is the blood coursing through our veins. Art distinguishes between mankind and mechanoids. The death of art is the death of humanity. I feel the passion emanating from every one and can’t help but fall in love. I glance at the old woman and suddenly it occurs to me how much of an impact she’s made on me with such a short encounter. But, that’s all it takes sometimes- an exchange of a few words between souls.
The concrete wall is no more itself,
It carries the vitality of being spotted by elusive colours;
Colours that prove existence.
I gained back my soul today.

runs.text: ফিরে এসো।
প্রিয় প্রতিমা,
হঠাৎ খুব চিঠি লিখতে ইচ্ছে হলো। ভাবলাম, তোকে একটা চিঠি লিখি। তবুও জানিস, এবার কিন্তু আমি এই চিঠির
উত্তর আশা করছি। গত কয়েকবার তুই আমাকে কোনো উত্তর দিসনি। এতে আমার মন খারাপ হয়েছে। আগে তো
এমন করতিস না। কত কথা বলতিস আমাকে, আর এখন কয়েক সপ্তাহ হয়ে গেল, তোর সঙ্গে ঠিকমতো কথাই হয়
না। তুই কি আমার ওপর রাগ করেছিস?
জানিস, আজকাল লোকেরা আমাকে পাগল বলে। আমি নাকি একা একা কথা বলি। মা খুব কষ্ট করে তাদের কথা
শোনে। এটা কোনো কথা? আমি তো তোর সঙ্গেই কথা বলি। এতে পাগলামির কী আছে? তুই যে আমার সঙ্গে কথা
বলিস, সেটা কি ওরা শুনতে পায় না?
বাদ দে। সেদিন আমি আমাদের পুরোনো স্কুলব্যাগটা হাতে নিলাম। কত দিন যে ওটা খোলা হয়নি! খুলে দেখি, তোর
পছন্দের কলমটা। কলমটা যত্ন করে তুলে রেখেছি। তুই এলে ফেরত দেব। তুই আবার অন্যের জিনিস হারিয়ে গেলে
আমার ওপর দোষ চাপিয়ে দিবি, আমি জানি। ছোটবেলা থেকেই তোর এই স্বভাবটা গেল না।
জানিস, আজ খুব পুকুরপাড়ে যেতে মন চাইছিল। আমার এখনও মনে আছে, শেষ যেদিন গিয়েছিলাম, তুই আমাকে
ছেড়ে সাঁতার কাটতে নেমে পড়েছিলি। কতবার তোকে ডাক দিলাম, তুই শুনলি না! একবারও ফিরে তাকালি না।
তোর ওপর সেদিন কী রাগটাই না হয়েছিল আমার! কিন্তু তুই তো জানিস, আমি বেশিক্ষণ তোর ওপর রাগ করে
থাকতে পারি না।
যাক, পুরোনো কথা আর না বলি। তোর সঙ্গে সেই কবে কথা হয়েছে, তারপর থেকে কত সপ্তাহ পেরিয়ে গেছে। তুই
আর একবারও আমার কাছে এলি না। এখন তোকে বলার জন্য কত কথা জমে আছে, অথচ তোকে কোথাও খুঁজে
পাই না। আমার ওপর রাগ করলি? নাকি আমাকে ভুলেই গেলি? ফিরে আয় না, তোকে অনেক কথা বলার আছে।
জানিস, মা-ও আজকাল কেমন অদ্ভুত হয়ে গেছে। কেউ তোর কথা তুললে মায়ের চোখ দুটো কেমন ভিজে ওঠে।
মাঝে মাঝে দেখি, আঁচল চাপা দিয়ে কাঁদতে থাকে। আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলেও কিছুই বলে না। একদিন তোকে নিয়ে
কথা বলতে গিয়ে মা হঠাৎ থেমে গেল। আমার দিকে কেমন করে যেন তাকাল, তারপর আমাকে জড়িয়ে ধরে কাঁদতে
লাগল। আমি কিছুই বুঝলাম না। তুই তো আছিস, তবু সবাই এমন করে কেন বলে, বল তো?
ফিরে আয়, বোন। মাঝরাতে ঘুম ভেঙে গেলে হাত বাড়িয়ে তোকে খুঁজি। আগে তোকে ডাকলেই পেতাম। এখন
ডাকলেও কেউ সাড়া দেয় না। ঘরটা কেমন অচেনা লাগে। বুকের ভেতরটা কেমন হিম হয়ে ওঠে, এক অচেনা অশান্তি
ঘিরে ধরে আমাকে। কখনো কখনো মনে হয়, তুই হয়তো পাশের ঘরে আছিস, আমার ওপর রাগ করে চুপ করে বসে
আছিস। আমি তোকে ডাকতে গিয়েও থেমে যাই।কেন জানি না, ইদানীং তোর সঙ্গে কথা বলতে গেলেই সব কেমন
গুলিয়ে যায়।
মাঝে মাঝে মনে হয়, তুই ফিরে এলে সব ঠিক হয়ে যাবে। মা আবার হাসবে, আর বাড়িটা আবার কোলাহলে ভরে
উঠবে। তুই আবার আমার সঙ্গে ঝগড়া করবি, আমার জিনিসপত্র নিয়ে পালাবি। আর আমার যত অভিমান জমে আছে,
সব বলব। একটাও বাদ দেব না। তুই শুধু একবার ফিরে আয়, বোন।
জানিস, মাঝে মাঝে আয়নায় নিজের মুখ দেখলে কেমন অদ্ভুত লাগে। ছোটবেলা থেকে সবাই বলত, আমাদের
দুজনকে নাকি আলাদা করে চেনাই যায় না। তুই হাসলে আমিও হাসতাম, তুই কাঁদলে আমারও কান্না পেত। আমরা
নাকি একে অপরের প্রতিচ্ছবি। কথাটা মনে পড়লে আজকাল নিজেকে কেমন একা লাগে।
বল তো, তুই যদি আমার প্রতিচ্ছবি হোস, তবে তুই কোথায় হারিয়ে গেলি?
ফিরে আয়। আমি আর কোনো অভিযোগ করব না। তোর কলমটা ফেরত দেব, তোর সব কথা শুনব। শুধু একবার
আমার পাশে এসে বস।
আর একবার ফিরে আয়।
ইতি,
তোর প্রতিচ্ছবি।

content: ফিরে এসো।
প্রিয় প্রতিমা,

হঠাৎ খুব চিঠি লিখতে ইচ্ছে হলো। ভাবলাম, তোকে একটা চিঠি লিখি। তবুও জানিস, এবার কিন্তু আমি এই চিঠির উত্তর আশা করছি। গত কয়েকবার তুই আমাকে কোনো উত্তর দিসনি। এতে আমার মন খারাপ হয়েছে। আগে তো এমন করতিস না। কত কথা বলতিস আমাকে, আর এখন কয়েক সপ্তাহ হয়ে গেল, তোর সঙ্গে ঠিকমতো কথাই হয় না। তুই কি আমার ওপর রাগ করেছিস?

জানিস, আজকাল লোকেরা আমাকে পাগল বলে। আমি নাকি একা একা কথা বলি। মা খুব কষ্ট করে তাদের কথা শোনে। এটা কোনো কথা? আমি তো তোর সঙ্গেই কথা বলি। এতে পাগলামির কী আছে? তুই যে আমার সঙ্গে কথা বলিস, সেটা কি ওরা শুনতে পায় না?

বাদ দে। সেদিন আমি আমাদের পুরোনো স্কুলব্যাগটা হাতে নিলাম। কত দিন যে ওটা খোলা হয়নি! খুলে দেখি, তোর পছন্দের কলমটা। কলমটা যত্ন করে তুলে রেখেছি। তুই এলে ফেরত দেব। তুই আবার অন্যের জিনিস হারিয়ে গেলে আমার ওপর দোষ চাপিয়ে দিবি, আমি জানি। ছোটবেলা থেকেই তোর এই স্বভাবটা গেল না।

জানিস, আজ খুব পুকুরপাড়ে যেতে মন চাইছিল। আমার এখনও মনে আছে, শেষ যেদিন গিয়েছিলাম, তুই আমাকে ছেড়ে সাঁতার কাটতে নেমে পড়েছিলি। কতবার তোকে ডাক দিলাম, তুই শুনলি না! একবারও ফিরে তাকালি না। তোর ওপর সেদিন কী রাগটাই না হয়েছিল আমার! কিন্তু তুই তো জানিস, আমি বেশিক্ষণ তোর ওপর রাগ করে থাকতে পারি না।

যাক, পুরোনো কথা আর না বলি। তোর সঙ্গে সেই কবে কথা হয়েছে, তারপর থেকে কত সপ্তাহ পেরিয়ে গেছে। তুই আর একবারও আমার কাছে এলি না। এখন তোকে বলার জন্য কত কথা জমে আছে, অথচ তোকে কোথাও খুঁজে পাই না। আমার ওপর রাগ করলি? নাকি আমাকে ভুলেই গেলি? ফিরে আয় না, তোকে অনেক কথা বলার আছে।

জানিস, মা-ও আজকাল কেমন অদ্ভুত হয়ে গেছে। কেউ তোর কথা তুললে মায়ের চোখ দুটো কেমন ভিজে ওঠে। মাঝে মাঝে দেখি, আঁচল চাপা দিয়ে কাঁদতে থাকে। আমি জিজ্ঞেস করলেও কিছুই বলে না। একদিন তোকে নিয়ে কথা বলতে গিয়ে মা হঠাৎ থেমে গেল। আমার দিকে কেমন করে যেন তাকাল, তারপর আমাকে জড়িয়ে ধরে কাঁদতে লাগল। আমি কিছুই বুঝলাম না। তুই তো আছিস, তবু সবাই এমন করে কেন বলে, বল তো?

ফিরে আয়, বোন। মাঝরাতে ঘুম ভেঙে গেলে হাত বাড়িয়ে তোকে খুঁজি। আগে তোকে ডাকলেই পেতাম। এখন ডাকলেও কেউ সাড়া দেয় না। ঘরটা কেমন অচেনা লাগে। বুকের ভেতরটা কেমন হিম হয়ে ওঠে, এক অচেনা অশান্তি ঘিরে ধরে আমাকে। কখনো কখনো মনে হয়, তুই হয়তো পাশের ঘরে আছিস, আমার ওপর রাগ করে চুপ করে বসে
আছিস। আমি তোকে ডাকতে গিয়েও থেমে যাই।কেন জানি না, ইদানীং তোর সঙ্গে কথা বলতে গেলেই সব কেমন গুলিয়ে যায়।

মাঝে মাঝে মনে হয়, তুই ফিরে এলে সব ঠিক হয়ে যাবে। মা আবার হাসবে, আর বাড়িটা আবার কোলাহলে ভরে উঠবে। তুই আবার আমার সঙ্গে ঝগড়া করবি, আমার জিনিসপত্র নিয়ে পালাবি। আর আমার যত অভিমান জমে আছে, সব বলব। একটাও বাদ দেব না। তুই শুধু একবার ফিরে আয়, বোন।

জানিস, মাঝে মাঝে আয়নায় নিজের মুখ দেখলে কেমন অদ্ভুত লাগে। ছোটবেলা থেকে সবাই বলত, আমাদের দুজনকে নাকি আলাদা করে চেনাই যায় না। তুই হাসলে আমিও হাসতাম, তুই কাঁদলে আমারও কান্না পেত। আমরা নাকি একে অপরের প্রতিচ্ছবি। কথাটা মনে পড়লে আজকাল নিজেকে কেমন একা লাগে।
বল তো, তুই যদি আমার প্রতিচ্ছবি হোস, তবে তুই কোথায় হারিয়ে গেলি?
ফিরে আয়। আমি আর কোনো অভিযোগ করব না। তোর কলমটা ফেরত দেব, তোর সব কথা শুনব। শুধু একবার আমার পাশে এসে বস।
আর একবার ফিরে আয়।
ইতি, তোর প্রতিচ্ছবি।

title: I would love to drown
author: Eggman
imageAlt: Cover image for I would love to drown

runs.text: I would love to drown
How dare you call to me,
O mystically silent ocean.
Your lustre,
Your magnificence,
Your silence,
Obscure and divine.
Your call, o so seductive,
Taunting me with that cold embrace-
Far from all the agonising heat of the world.
Yet, did my God not tell you I cannot swim?
Yet, I yearn for your embrace.
O to be so far from this benign existence.
O to be set free.
O how the unknown caged bird,
Comes and goes.

title: Ode to verse
author: Eggman
imageAlt: Cover image for Ode to verse

runs.text: Ode to verse
Dearest verse,
I hope you will forever stay as warm as the first time I met you. But nowadays I question your
warmth, you are a paradox; both sadistic and seductive.
O verse, how I bleed—
My untold desires,
My ruthless indecency,
My lustrous premonition,
In each dot and comma.
Only for no answer.
Foolish I am, seeking a cure for an ailment in words and syllables. An apothecary would laugh
at my face.
Dearest verse you are so cold. So obscurely cold. Is it you who leaches the warmth from me?
Yet so addicted I am to you, each time the world tries to crucify me, your embrace, it hides me
from the mobs.
Their pitchforks, just how can they never reach me in your bosom?
Your bosom, just how is it always so serene?
Yet, you kept me for so long, I no longer even recognise the man in the reflection.
Where is it?
His innocence,
His voice,
The light in his eyes,
The clearness of his soul,
Where?
I will never not come back to you. Just how have I made you the last string holding my
humanity and faith together.
Dearest verse,
How have I let you become my prayer?
How beautifully you are destroying me.

title: Ruins
author: Eggman

runs.text: Ruins
The grand walls,
The lustrous mosaics,
The pristine pillars,
All of them, rotting,
Detritus.
Yet, in the detestable ruin of these great halls,
How is the scent of mercy still lingering?
Erato, why do I still hear the melodies of your harp?
Persephone, your spouse,
Why is he wandering here?
Eleos, is it you I see dancing in the corner of my eye?
Why does this rain not stop?
Have these once great halls not been cleansed yet?
The wind, its breeze,
How is it so heavy?
